done.why: I died a fourth time, to a grue on the walk from the stair to the barren area with no light. The voice in the void said goodnight and the game told me nothing more would happen. My own play put me there: I drowned my lantern testing the lake, left the torch in the Scenic Vista, jumped off the broken aqueduct, and then walked around blind.

about: An old man is testing you at the bottom of an endless stair, in the ruins of an underground empire. To be worthy of him you gather the things he carries in your dream: his staff, amulet, key, and presumably a ring and a book. You get them by being kind as well as clever. You let a thief take a chest, feed a starving old man, and fight a hooded figure who fights exactly like you. A lot of it is sad. There's a broken aqueduct, a cold lake that takes whatever you hold, and a table that keeps showing you other places.

ending.what: A losing ending. After my fourth death the voice said 'perhaps it has been another that I have been seeking. Good night, oh worthy adventurer!' and left me in the Void. I never got past the secret door in the Engravings Room.

moments.note: 'The stairs are endless.' The stair has a dry little joke in it, and the description before that was lovely.
I tied the rope to the chest and a man at the top hauled it up, chuckling, and left me stranded on the ledge.
About eight waits on the ledge before he came back. The flavor text was good but it repeated word for word every time.
He pulled me up and gave me the plain wooden staff, which I recognized from the dream.
I gave the bread to the old man, he pointed at a secret door, and then he was gone.
Taking the stairs down turned me back. The game told me plainly I wasn't ready yet, and that there was no word or key left for me in that room. Clear and kind.
Diving in the icy lake for the shiny thing, with a hungry fish around, and coming up with the amulet.
Touching the Scenic Vista table on IV dropped me onto a sacrificial altar and I died at once. The prison cell vision afterwards was striking.
The sword came out of nowhere, glowing, to meet the hooded figure who fights the way I do.
The fight was long and swingy. I backed off when I was badly hurt, and the game had already told me that was fine, which helped.
I tested whether the lantern could cross the lake. It hissed and died for good. The game had warned me and I did it anyway.
My trick worked. I dropped the torch in the Damp Passage, rode the table there on III, picked it up, and the wind blew me back to the Vista with it. That was the best moment I had.
Room 8, lit by the torch, had a can of Frobozz Magic Grue Repellent in it.
The repellent got me through the dark to the Key Room, where a shape-changing key lay in a shaft of light.
I went down the manhole into the aqueduct. The arch was broken, the hole above was too high and the waterfall couldn't be climbed. I seemed to be trapped, so I jumped.
I sent a batch of moves in the dark at once and a grue ate me before I could stop.
One more death in the dark and the game ended for good, in the Void.

wished: I wanted to pull the sword from the rock myself. It just turned up at the fight.
I wanted a way out of the aqueduct once I'd dropped through the manhole, or some warning that it was a trap.
I wanted to talk to the thief properly. He ignored everything I tried.
I wanted a dry way to carry fire across the lake, or a fair hint that the torch had to stay on the Vista side.
I wanted to see where the passage past the hooded figure went, and what the earthquake had changed.
I wanted to get past the climbing passage and the squeeze east of the Creepy Crawl.

lines.line: The stairs are endless; that is rather the point of them.
lines.why: A dry, confident voice from the very start.

lines.line: It has the look of an old friend who has followed you somewhere it would rather not have come.
lines.why: It made me care about the lantern, so drowning it later actually hurt.

lines.line: not for anything left undone up here, no word or key or deed this room is waiting on, but for what is still to be gathered in places you have not yet been.
lines.why: A gate that told me exactly what kind of thing was missing without spelling out the answer.

lines.line: A fight that is going badly can be walked away from, into the dark, where it will not follow; wounds mend with time, on both sides
lines.why: A fair nudge in the middle of a swingy fight.

lines.line: It is a flame for dry land: it will go wherever you carry it on foot, and the lake would put it out for good
lines.why: This was the clue that made the torch puzzle readable.

lines.line: the pale surface, angled toward you, seems to lean a little nearer as it goes, the way a thing does that would rather be touched than looked at.
lines.why: A creepy invitation, and the first time I took it, it killed me.

lines.line: perhaps it has been another that I have been seeking. Good night, oh worthy adventurer!
lines.why: A melancholy goodbye after I'd failed.

fun.why: Several really satisfying puzzles: the bread and the secret door, diving for the amulet, and above all bringing the torch back to the Vista by riding the table. It soured near the end when I lost my light and kept dying.

engagement.why: I wanted to see every place and the world kept giving me new ones: the cliff, the beach, the lake shores, rooms seen through the table, the key room, the aqueduct. Long stretches of waiting at the ledge and at the Vista dragged.

difficulty.why: It's fair about the lake and the torch, but unforgiving. Losing the lantern, the aqueduct dead end and darkness that kills you add up fast, and before I knew it the game was over. I didn't see the death limit coming.

interestingness.why: The hooded figure who mirrors you, the thief who still gives you the staff, the time-cycling table that sends you to far-off rooms, and the gate that tells you you're not yet worthy. All of it sits on one theme of proving yourself.

prose.why: Warm, wry and sad. The lantern, the aqueduct ('the saddest thing you have seen underground') and the cold lake that 'would open your hands for you' all stuck with me. The only flaw was the ledge-wait text repeating word for word.
